summaries.example: Imagine you see a tiny insect on a path. A Jaina lesson might encourage you to notice it and step around it instead of hurting it. This shows care for living beings and careful self-control.
summaries.summary: Jaina philosophy is a way of thinking connected with Jainism. It teaches that each living being has a conscious self and that this self is covered or limited by karmic matter. People seek liberation, or freedom, by changing themselves rather than trying only to change the outside world. They practice non-violence, self-control, non-attachment, meditation, and other forms of renunciation. Jaina thinkers also describe the world carefully: selves and non-self matter are different, yet they exist together. They say that the same thing can remain in one respect while changing in another. This helps explain the Jaina teaching that reality has many sides. A good understanding therefore requires careful distinctions instead of treating every question as having only one simple answer.
key_ideas: Jaina philosophy asks how people can free themselves from repeated rebirths and suffering.
Careful behavior is central. Harm can be physical, spoken, mental, direct, or even something we allow.
Jaina thinkers say that living beings have selves, while other things are non-self.
The self can gain clearer knowledge by reducing attachment, harmful actions, and karmic matter.
Things can stay the same in one way while changing in another way.
Because things have many sides, a careful answer may depend on which side or viewpoint is being considered.
summaries.why_it_matters: This philosophy gives serious attention to how everyday choices affect other living beings. It also teaches intellectual care: before saying that something is simply one way or another, we can ask what aspect, time, or viewpoint we mean. Its ideas connect ethics, knowledge, and a picture of reality into one system.

important_terms.definition: A religious and philosophical tradition that teaches careful living, non-violence, self-control, and a path toward freedom.
The idea of not harming living beings through actions, words, or thoughts.
The living, conscious self that experiences, acts, and can become free from things that block its knowledge.
A very subtle kind of matter that, according to Jaina philosophy, sticks to the self and blocks its natural abilities.
Freedom from the cycle of rebirth and from the blocks that keep the self from knowing clearly.

questions_to_think_about: Why might careful attention be needed before taking even a small action?
Can someone harm another person through words or thoughts, not only through physical actions?
How can something be both lasting and changing?
Why might looking at more than one side of a question help us understand it?

summaries.example: Suppose a clay pot is newly shaped. A Jaina philosopher can say that it exists as clay, because its substance continues, but did not previously exist in that particular shape and use. The pot therefore shows persistence and change together. A statement about it must specify which aspect is being discussed.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry presents Jaina philosophy as a systematic attempt to understand liberation, reality, and knowledge together. Its ethical path centers on renunciation, non-violence, non-attachment, and the purification of the self. Jainas describe karma as subtle matter that becomes connected with a conscious self and obstructs its knowledge and capacities. Liberation is therefore both moral and epistemic: reducing passions and karmic bondage makes unobstructed cognition possible. Metaphysically, Jaina thinkers distinguish innumerable selves from non-self substances, including matter, space, media of motion and rest, and, in some accounts, time. They defend an active self so that actions can have genuine moral significance. In epistemology, they develop accounts of perception, testimony, inference, and omniscient knowledge. Their realism and doctrine of many-sidedness hold that objects have multiple real aspects. Thus, a claim can be true under one specification and false under another without making reality incoherent. The doctrine of perspectives gives a structured account of how different philosophical systems may grasp different aspects while becoming mistaken when they absolutize one perspective.
key_ideas: Jaina ethics is a program of renunciation aimed at ending rebirth and separating the self from karmic matter.
Ahiṃsā extends beyond avoiding direct physical injury: responsibility can include delegated, permitted, verbal, and mental forms of harm.
Jaina metaphysics is dualist: conscious selves and non-self substances are fundamentally distinct, while karma is treated as a subtle material association.
The self is active and morally responsible, unlike views that make ultimate selves wholly passive or deny a persisting self.
Jaina realism holds that objects exist independently of our knowledge, but objects are complex and can be described from different perspectives.
Anekāntavāda explains persistence and change by distinguishing substance from changing modes; nayavāda organizes the standpoints used in making claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: Jaina philosophy links ethical discipline to theories of mind, matter, and knowledge rather than treating them as separate subjects. It offers a demanding model of non-violence and a sophisticated response to the problem of how things can persist while changing. Its many-sided approach also provides a way to study philosophical disagreement without assuming that every opposing view is simply meaningless or wholly correct.

important_terms.definition: The Jaina philosophical tradition, associated with the teachings of omniscient Jinas and developed in texts, monastic communities, and lay practices.
The ethical commitment to avoid harming living beings through direct or indirect physical, verbal, or mental action.
The conscious, active self, distinct from non-self substances and capable of knowledge, responsibility, and liberation.
Subtle matter that becomes associated with the self, especially through passions, and obstructs knowledge and other natural capacities.
The view that reality has multiple aspects, so apparently opposing claims may each be correct when made with respect to different conditions.
A theory of epistemic standpoints that classifies different ways of attending to or describing a complex object.
Knowledge gained by reasoning from an established evidence-property to a target-property through an invariable connection.
The condition in which karmic obstructions have been removed and the self manifests unobstructed knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Does extending responsibility to actions that permit or delegate harm make an ethical theory stronger, more demanding, or both?
Why does Jaina moral responsibility require an active and persisting self?
Can a thing be permanent as a substance but impermanent in its modes without contradiction?
How might many-sidedness help explain disagreement between philosophical traditions?
What should make a teacher or testimony authoritative: the speaker's qualities, the argument's internal support, or both?

summaries.example: Imagine a school garden where a student wants to clear weeds. A Jaina approach would first ask what living beings may be affected, whether the action is necessary, and whether it can be done with less harm. The decision is not judged only by the result: intention, carelessness, and whether the harm was direct or permitted may also matter.
summaries.summary: Jaina philosophy connects a way of life with a theory of reality and knowledge. Its central goal is liberation from repeated rebirths. A person moves toward liberation through renunciation, self-control, meditation, non-attachment, and especially ahiṃsā, or non-violence. Jaina ethics is unusually demanding because harm may be physical, verbal, or mental, and responsibility may include causing harm indirectly or approving it. Living beings are understood to have jīvas, or conscious selves. Karma is described as subtle matter that becomes associated with the self, particularly through passions and mistaken attitudes, and that blocks knowledge and other abilities. Right conduct can stop this inflow and gradually remove what is already attached. Jaina metaphysics distinguishes self from non-self and treats the self as active and responsible. Jaina epistemology studies how knowledge works, including inference and testimony from reliable teachers. Its best-known philosophical contribution is many-sidedness. A thing can be enduring in its underlying substance while changing in its particular states. Therefore, a statement may be correct when carefully limited to a certain time, property, or standpoint. The doctrine of perspectives develops this idea into a method for understanding different philosophical views.
key_ideas: The Jaina path changes the person through renunciation rather than mainly changing the surrounding world.
Non-violence applies to many forms of life, including very small forms, and can involve what one does, says, thinks, permits, or asks others to do.
Jaina thinkers distinguish the conscious self from non-self matter and explain karma as a material obstruction.
The self remains responsible for action, so Jaina philosophy rejects views that make the self completely passive or deny an enduring self.
Jaina philosophers combine realism with many-sidedness: the world exists independently, but it cannot always be captured by one unqualified statement.
Knowledge can come through perception, testimony, inference, and, in advanced cases, higher forms of cognition.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry shows how an ethical rule can shape an entire philosophy. If every living being matters, people need detailed ideas about life, action, intention, knowledge, and responsibility. The Jaina response to disagreement is also valuable: instead of ignoring differences, it asks which aspect each view notices and whether that aspect has been treated as the whole truth.

important_terms.definition: A South Asian religious and philosophical tradition whose teachings emphasize liberation, non-violence, self-control, and careful investigation of reality.
Avoiding harm to living beings and developing constant care in physical, spoken, and mental behavior.
A conscious living self that acts, experiences results, and can develop clearer knowledge.
Subtle matter that becomes attached to the self and helps produce limitations, rebirth, and distorted understanding.
The process of stopping new karmic matter from entering and removing karmic matter already connected with the self.
The claim that a real thing can have several aspects, so different qualified descriptions may all be accurate.
A conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence that is necessarily connected with what one wants to establish.

questions_to_think_about: Why would a theory of non-violence include actions that someone allows or orders, not just actions they perform themselves?
What is gained by describing karma as a kind of matter rather than only as a moral score?
Can two statements that seem opposite both be reasonable if they refer to different aspects of one thing?
Why might a philosophical tradition value both debate and authoritative teaching?
How could a careful viewpoint prevent an argument from becoming too extreme?
